facts.statement: Qinornis is known from a single fossil specimen found in the Fangou Formation in Luonan County, China.
facts.quote: It is known from a single fossil specimen consisting of a partial hind limb and foot, which was found in Fangou Formation deposits in Luonan County, China.

facts.statement: Qinornis lived during the early to mid-Paleocene epoch, approximately 61 million years ago.
facts.quote: Qinornis is a genus of extinct ornithuran from the early-mid-Paleocene epoch (late Danian age), about 61 million years ago.

facts.statement: The bones of Qinornis display uniquely primitive characteristics for its age, leading researchers to debate whether it was a juvenile modern bird or an adult non-neornithine bird that survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
facts.quote: The bones show uniquely primitive characteristics for its age, and its describer considered that it was either a juvenile of a modern bird group or, if an adult, the only known non-neornithine bird to have survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.

facts.statement: Unusually for a bird of its recent age, the foot bones of Qinornis are not completely fused.
facts.quote: Unusually for such a recent bird, the bones of the foot are not completely fused to one another.

facts.statement: Mayr argued in 2007 that the Qinornis specimen was an adult because the distal tarsalia were fused with the metatarsalia and lacked the blurred surfaces typical of growing juvenile neornithine birds.
facts.quote: In 2007, Mayr examined the bones and concluded that they represented an adult, and probably did come from a non-neornithine bird similar to Apsaravis "because the distal tarsalia are completely fused with the metatarsalia and the articular ends of the tarsometatarsus do not exhibit the blurred surfaces characteristic for the growing bones of juvenile neornithine birds."

facts.statement: Longrich and colleagues (2011) questioned Mayr's conclusion, suggesting the bones might belong to a juvenile, while also noting it was not impossible that some archaic birds persisted beyond the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Longrich y otros colegas (2011) pusieron en duda esta afirmación, señalando que existe la posibilidad de que los huesos pertenecieran a un juvenil, pero también señalaron que no era imposible que algunas aves "arcaicas" hayan persistido más allá del período Cretácico durante algún tiempo

facts.statement: The genus Qinornis was described by Xue in 1995.
The genus Qinornis was named by Xue in 1995.
The type species of the genus Qinornis is Qinornis paleocenica.
Qinornis belongs to the parent group Ornithurae.
The time range for Qinornis is from 66 to 61.66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Danian to Danian (66 to 61.66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: In 2007, Mayr concluded that the Qinornis specimen represented an adult non-neornithine bird similar to Apsaravis.
rejected.quote: In 2007, Mayr examined the bones and concluded that they represented an adult, and probably did come from a non-neornithine bird similar to Apsaravis.
